#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when you need a one-off patch*
This scenario shows the direct way to use a private repository: instead of a vendor BOM, the build names the patched version explicitly in `libraryDependencies`. It is simpler than SB16 and suits one-off patches, at the cost of being an ordinary declaration with an ordinary declaration's weaknesses.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **sbt 1.12**, which uses the **Coursier** resolver (the default since sbt 1.3). On sbt 1.x the older Ivy engine can still be selected with `useCoursier := false`; under Ivy, resolution edge cases differ and Ivy-only settings such as `conflictManager` apply (Coursier ignores them). `dependencyTree` is built in since **sbt 1.4**; earlier versions need the sbt-dependency-graph plugin. sbt 2.0 (June 2026) keeps these resolution rules, removes the Ivy opt-out, adds native BOM import, and turns Test-configuration eviction warnings into errors; the demos here target sbt 1.x.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    subgraph Public Repos
        SpringBoot["spring-boot-starter:2.5.14 (EOL)"]
    end
    subgraph Private Repo
        PatchedStarter["spring-boot-starter:2.5.14.ACME"]
    end
    Root[Project Root] -- declares --> PatchedStarter
```

The `build.sbt` adds the private repository to `resolvers` and declares the patched version directly.

```{.scala include="build.sbt" snippet="repo-and-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
Declaring the patched version from the private repository guarantees the build uses that artifact.

#### ! Actual
It does, here, because nothing else in the graph asks for `spring-boot-starter`. The declaration is still only a request (SB4): if a transitive dependency asked for a higher public version, highest-wins would evict `2.5.14.ACME` for it, and the patch would silently disappear. Note that `2.5.14.ACME` sorts *above* `2.5.14` for Coursier, which is why it also wins against a transitive request for the plain public release.

#### ! Why
A private resolver makes the artifact available; a direct declaration asks for it. That is enough while the request is uncontested. The BOM emulation in SB16 uses `dependencyOverrides` precisely so that the patched version is *forced* rather than requested, which is the difference between a one-off patch and a policy.

#### ! Fix
*   **One-off patch:** the direct declaration, as shown, with a comment naming the CVE or vendor ticket.
*   **Policy:** promote the pin to `dependencyOverrides` (SB16) so a transitive request cannot evict it.
*   **Detect drift:** `sbt evicted` after any dependency change, and a CI assertion that `2.5.14.ACME` is on `Runtime / fullClasspath`.

#### ! Risk
* LOW One patched artifact, commented, in a graph where nothing else requests it.
* MEDIUM Several patched artifacts declared directly; one of them loses a future eviction and nobody notices.
* HIGH A patched version string that sorts *below* the public one; the public release wins every conflict and the patch never applies.

#### ! Control
Keep private-repository pins in one block with the reason for each. Review `sbt evicted` as part of every dependency upgrade so a lost patch shows up in the pull request, not in production.

#### ! Check
**Fast check:** `sbt "show externalDependencyClasspath"`

**What to look for:** `spring-boot-starter-2.5.14.ACME.jar` on the classpath, from the private repository.

**Conclusion:** A direct declaration is enough while it is uncontested; make it an override when it must hold.

#### ! Scales
Direct patches do not scale: each is a request that any new dependency can out-vote, and each needs its own comment and its own check. Past two or three, move to the override list of SB16 and manage them as a set.

#### ! Takeaway
A direct declaration from a private repository is the simplest way to use a patched artifact, and the weakest. Use it for one-offs; use `dependencyOverrides` for policy.

#### ! Wild

In December 2021, Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) sent every JVM team to the same place: pin `log4j-core` to the patched release, that day, ahead of whatever the frameworks shipped. In sbt that meant a direct declaration of `2.17.0` and, for anyone who checked `sbt evicted` the following week, the discovery that a transitive from a logging bridge still asked for `2.14.1` and had been quietly out-voted only because `2.17.0` happened to be higher. The teams that promoted the pin to `dependencyOverrides` did not have to think about it again when `2.17.1` followed.
